title: The Desert Bullseye Visible From Orbit 👁️
hook_sentence: Visible from space as a massive desert landmark, concentric rings span the sands.
narration_script: Visible from space as a massive desert landmark, concentric rings span the sands. Geological field surveys record the feature at 25 miles (40 km) across, though satellite observations describe it as spanning almost 31 miles (50 km). The eroded dome formed when subsurface igneous intrusion deformed overlying sedimentary rock. Initially considered an extraterrestrial impact crater, the theory was disproved in 1969 when suspected shock minerals were identified as mislabeled barite. In October 2022, the International Union of Geological Sciences designated this formation among the world's first 100 official geological heritage sites. The colossal eroded bullseye endures as an unmistakable beacon across the sands.
closing_sentence: The colossal eroded bullseye endures as an unmistakable beacon across the sands.
caption:
A colossal concentric bullseye marks the vast Sahara desert from space.
🌍 Near Ouadane on the Adrar Plateau of Mauritania, prehistoric hunters once traversed these ridges, leaving Stone Age tools dating between roughly 145,000 and 29,000 years ago. By one estimate, thousands of prehistoric stone burial mounds built in distinct architectural styles also line the formation's protruding dikes. Field geology confirms this ancient natural inland dome is not Plato's Atlantis. audits.claim: The Richat Structure is a massive concentric desert landmark in Mauritania visible from orbit.
audits.note: Supported by Q1, Q4, and Q7, which confirm the structure's concentric rings and that it is a circular landmark visible from space.

audits.claim: The structure has an estimated diameter of 40 km (25 mi) to nearly 50 km (31 mi).
audits.note: Supported by Q3, Q4, Q5, and Q6, which record measurements of 40 kilometres (25 miles) across and diameters of roughly or almost 50 kilometres (30 miles).

audits.claim: The eroded dome formed when a subsurface igneous intrusion deformed overlying sedimentary rock layers.
audits.note: Directly supported by Q4, which states it is an eroded geological dome caused by a subsurface igneous intrusion deforming the overlying sedimentary rock layers into concentric rings.

audits.claim: Initially considered an impact structure, the impact theory was disproved in 1969 when suspected shock minerals were found to be misidentified barite.
audits.note: Supported by Q16, Q17, and Q18, which state that it was initially considered an impact structure, shock metamorphism was ruled out in the 1960s, and a 1969 analysis determined that barite had been misidentified as coesite.

audits.claim: In October 2022, the International Union of Geological Sciences selected the Richat Structure as one of the world's 100 geological heritage sites.
audits.note: Directly supported by Q19 and Q20.

audits.claim: The Richat Structure is located near Ouadane on the Adrar Plateau of Mauritania.
Stone Age tools found at the Richat Structure date to between approximately 145,000 and 29,000 years ago.
audits.note: Supported by Q22, which dates Middle Stone Age Aterian artifacts at the site to between around 145,000 and 29,000 years ago.

audits.claim: Thousands of stone burial mounds in various styles line the protruding dikes of the formation.
Geological analysis contradicts claims identifying the inland Richat Structure as Plato's Atlantis.
audits.note: Supported by Q24 and Q25, which note that claims identifying it as Atlantis are unsubstantiated fringe claims and contradicted by its ancient geological origin and inland desert location.

audits.claim: Carbonatite rocks at the formation have been dated to having cooled between 94 and 104 million years ago.
